BACKGROUND AND AIM: Geospatial analyses integrate location-based sociodemographic data, offering a

promising approach to investigate the impact of social determinants on acute pancreatitis (AP) outcomes.  This study

aimed to examine the association of social vulnerability index (SVI) and its constituent 16 attributes in 4 domains

(socioeconomic status, household composition and disability, minority status and language, and housing type and

transportation), with outcomes of patients with AP.

METHODS: This study included AP patients hospitalized between 1/1/2008 and 12/31/2018 and recorded their

demographics and clinical outcomes.  Physical addresses were geocoded to determine SVI, a composite variable which

was ranked and divided into quartiles (I to IV: IV representing the highest vulnerability).

RESULT: In 824 patients [age of 53.0±10 years and 48.2% females], with 993 AP-related hospitalizations, we noted

significantly higher prevalence of no/federal/state insurance (P<0.001) and racial minorities (P<0.001) in patients

residing in communities with higher SVI. A non-significant trend of higher 30-day admission rate amongst patients

from higher SVI regions (III/IV: 27(18.0%)/31(18.9%) vs. I/II: 40(13.8%)/36(16.3%); p=0.49) was noted. We

observed a significant association of alcohol withdrawal with residence in areas with higher SVI despite adjustment

for age, body mass index, and comorbidities (OR:1.62[95%CI:1.19-2.22]; p= 0.003). However, we observed no

association of SVI with severity of AP, inpatient opioid use, length of stay, and mortality.

CONCLUSION: We noted significantly higher alcohol withdrawal in patients residing in areas with higher SVI ranks

although AP severity and other outcomes lacked significant association with SVI. Given our findings further

investigation of various social determinants of health in AP is warranted in large sized prospective studies.

KEYWORDS: Acute Pancreatitis, Geospatial Disparity, Alcohol Withdrawal

## INTRODUCTION:

Acute Pancreatitis (AP) is an inflammatory pancreatic disorder characterized by unpredictable outcomes and in severe

cases, a substantial mortality rate of up to 20%.1, 2 Annually, AP accounts for a large proportion of gastrointestinal-

related hospital admissions: 288,220 hospitalizations in the United States as compared to 530,855 cases of

gastrointestinal bleeding. 3  In the United States alone, AP exerts a substantial economic impact, with annual health

spending exceeding $2.5 billion and rising globally.4 The burden of AP is rising, as reflected by the annual percent

change of 3.1% which may be attributable to improved clinical awareness of the condition, better diagnostic

techniques, and exposure to attributable risk factors (e.g. alcohol use, smoking, etc.).3,5 Goal-directed treatment,

including fluid resuscitation, is noted to be  most beneficial within the first 12-24 hours of presentation.6

Like other health conditions such as acute coronary syndrome and reactive airway disease, overall severity

and outcomes of AP may be influenced by social determinants of health (SDOH).7, 8 The World Health Organization

defines SDOH as crucial factors that influence an individual's well-being, as they encompass the conditions in which

people are born, grow, live, work, and age.9 Important examples of SDOH include factors such as financial insecurity,

poor access to health care, neighborhood deprivation, and ethno-racial discrimination which have previously been

associated with adverse health outcomes.10 Many of the SDOH indicators have complex relationships that are prone

to multicollinearity, making meaningful interpretation difficult. Thus, index-based approaches have emerged as

proxies to assess the impact of SDOH. These approaches incorporate factors intended to capture the multidimensional

nature of social determinants and their consequences for health outcomes.

Geospatial analysis has the potential to integrate location-based sociodemographic data with clinical

information offering a promising approach to better understand the care of AP patients. A geospatial approach may

also enable the identification of healthcare disparities, in part by making use of tools like the Social Vulnerability

Index (SVI), a composite measure of vulnerability to disasters or pandemics developed by the Centers for Disease

Control and Prevention (CDC).11 The SVI assigns each tract a raw score and a percentile rank (scored 0 to 1, with 1

representing the highest vulnerability). This multi-tiered measurement tool enables a global evaluation of a patient’s

tract-level SDOH based on four thematic subdomains: (1) socioeconomic status, 2) household composition and

disability, 3) minority status and language, and 4) housing type and transportation, in all comprising 16 social

## METHODS

Study Design and Setting

We conducted a retrospective, observational cohort study of patients diagnosed with AP and hospitalized at a tertiary

care center in the Boston area between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2018. This study was approved by the

Institutional Review Board (Protocol ID: 2018P000613). This study is reported in accordance with the Strengthening

the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline (Supplement 1). 12

Study Population:

Adult patients (aged 18 years or more) were identified through International Classification of Diseases, Ninth and

Tenth Revision codes 577.1 and K85.9. 13, 14 Electronic health records (EHRs) were then manually reviewed to confirm

the diagnosis of AP. The diagnosis of AP was based on Revised Atlanta classification (2 of the following during

hospitalization: typical abdominal pain, elevation of serum lipase level three times upper limit of normal, or evidence

of pancreatitis on cross-sectional imaging).15 Patients who were excluded were those who (1) carried a diagnosis of

chronic pancreatitis or pancreaticobiliary malignancy (2) lacked physical address, thus preventing geospatial coding.

Variable Definitions:

We reviewed the EHR to collect a wide range of data, including demographic, clinical, laboratory, radiological and

treatment information for patients with AP.16, 17 The demographic characteristics considered for each patient included

age, sex, race and ethnicity, active smoking or alcohol use, etiology of AP, insurance type and address. To accurately

locate each patient, we identified and geocoded their local street address. Additionally, we quantified the comorbidity

burden for each participant using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), which considered pre-existing conditions

such as diabetes, kidney disease, pulmonary, and cardiovascular comorbidities.18 The severity of presentation was

assessed using the BISAP score, a scoring system that utilizes blood urea nitrogen, impaired mental status, systemic

Additionally, we recorded systemic complications, including renal failure, respiratory failure, bacteremia,

and sepsis. We recorded the disposition of patients, including discharges to extended care facilities, the number of

readmissions within 30 days, as well as mortality within one year of original hospitalization. Furthermore, we collected

data on extra-pancreatic complications such as alcohol withdrawal, gastrointestinal bleeding, and delirium.

Geocoding and Social Vulnerability Index estimation:

We geocoded the residence of each patient and combined the resulting locations with the SVI metrics of the census

tracts in which they are located (Figure 1A; Supplement 2).11 Developed and published by the CDC, the SVI assigns

each tract a composite score which is then ranked based on percentile (ranging from 0 to 1 with 1 representing the

highest vulnerability). This tool enables an evaluation of four thematic subdomains: (1) socioeconomic status, 2)

household composition and disability, 3) minority status and language, and 4) housing type and transportation, in all

comprising 16 social attributes (Figure 1B). A comparison of patient demographics and health behaviors was

conducted across SVI quartiles I-IV, with quartile IV representing the highest vulnerability. Similarly, AP outcomes

were also analyzed based on SVI quartiles. Maps were created using ArcGIS Pro 2.7.0 (ESRI, Red-lands, CA).

Statistical Analysis:

Categorical data were presented as proportions, while continuous variables were reported as medians with interquartile

ranges. Statistical differences in categorical variables were assessed using Chi-square tests, while continuous variables

were analyzed using Kruskal-Wallis tests. AP outcome variables were the dependent variables and underwent

univariate logistic regression analysis to delineate their association with SVI.   Using a significance threshold of p-

## RESULTS:

The study enrolled 824 patients with AP, with a median age of 53.0(10) years and 48.18% of patients were female.

There were 993 AP-related hospitalization events, for which residential locations were divided into four SVI ranking

quartiles: Quartile I (n=338), Quartile II (n=271), Quartile III (n=182), and Quartile IV (n=202)

non-Hispanic Black, 108(13.1%) Hispanic, and 28(3.4%) non-Hispanic Asian patients. We noted that 8 (1.0%) patients

## DISCUSSION:

The morbidity of patients with AP, its complications, and overall mortality emphasize the need for conducting

comprehensive SDOH-based geospatial investigation.1, 2 In this study, we employ a novel approach of geocoding and

stratifying patients based on the SVI scores and ranked quartiles of their residential locations, a validated SDOH

grading tool, to assess unmeasured factors which may have an impact on patients hospitalized with AP. 11  Across SVI

quartiles, we evaluated geospatial disparities in clinical outcomes including disease severity, management, disposition,

and hospital readmissions.

In this retrospective cohort study, we noted that severity of clinical presentation lacked significant association

with residence in communities with social vulnerability, especially after adjusting for confounders (p=0.09). We

observed no significant difference in the local and systemic complications (e.g., respiratory failure, acute kidney injury,

and bacteremia) mortality, length of hospital stays, and rehabilitative requirements across SVI quartiles, but a trend

towards increased 30-day readmissions in the higher SVI quartiles. However, we observed higher odds of alcohol

withdrawal among patients with residing in communities with higher social vulnerability. A significant association of

alcohol withdrawal was noted with subdomains of SVI i.e. socioeconomic status, underrepresented minority status,

language, housing and transportation status. This finding is consistent with prior reporting of higher community

prevalence of alcohol withdrawal syndrome in single male patients in the lowest socioeconomic strata.21,22

Additionally, the subjective nature of assessing alcohol withdrawal (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment

protocol) can impede timely identification of this entity among patients with language barriers, further amplifying this

problem.23, 24 The impact of the physical environment and sociodemographic data based on the address of the patients

with AP has previously been investigated in national electronic healthcare record linkage cohort studies. In the UK,

the Social Deprivation Index, a multimodal marker involving seven demographic factors (poverty, education, single-

parent households, rented housing units, overcrowding, transport, unemployment), has been studied when considering

geospatial/physical infrastructure systems which may impact AP outcomes, as it includes additional parameters.

Our study is strengthened by a unique design for determining clinical outcomes of AP patients and well-

annotated clinical data. We relied on a manual review of individual charts, thus having high certainty of AP diagnosis.

We also geocoded the exact locations of each patient, which would not be possible using publicly available databases

due to privacy issues. Our conservative analysis investigated each trend with regression models which were adjusted

for demographics to reduce confounding. Aggregate geospatial socioeconomic variables have been compared with

individual-level data, and  were confirmed to have internal validity.26 This was demonstrated through higher minority

representation and percentage of uninsured/reliant on federal insurance in the patients with higher social vulnerability.

This was done since geographical aggregation of AP patients may predispose such studies to an ecological bias.27,26

Although we used insurance status, absence of individual socioeconomic data such as annual income constrained our

ability to account for this ecological fallacy.

The study is limited by its retrospective design and reliance on participants’ physical address, which fails to

capture change in residence or migration. Geocoding residential address also limits assessment of homeless population

which may be more at risk of adverse health outcomes. 28, 29 The study also lacks details on alcohol drinking behavior

and nutritional assessment of our patients, thus limiting the inference of its impact on the trend seen for alcohol

withdrawal. SVI though beneficial is not perfect. It is summation of various social attributes akin to principal

component analysis and may have some critical shortcomings regarding theoretical and internal consistency.30

Also, it was not unexpected that in our study AP patients residing in more socially vulnerable communities

did not have worse outcomes during their hospitalization, as the care provided to all is completely based on evidence-

based guidelines and decision tools, as previously reported.31 However, as noted, alcohol withdrawal rates were higher

in these patients, as this is dependent on drinking patterns outside the control of medical care givers. Moreover, being

aware of patients being discharged to areas with higher social vulnerability may be particularly important for their

recovery process. While we recommend careful consideration of the factors elevating community SVI scores in

optimizing discharge planning and follow-up strategies, we caution against oversimplified applications of SVI in risk

reduction efforts or healthcare policy aimed at addressing social determinants of health.30

determinants on AP outcomes. SVI can be used to identify sociocultural, economic, and institutional processes that

# Direct visualization of electric field-stimulated ion conduction in a potassium channel

**Authors:** BoRam Lee; K. Ian White; Michael Socolich; Margaret A. Klureza; Robert Henning; Vukica Srajer; Rama Ranganathan; Doeke R. Hekstra

**Affiliations:** 1Center for Physics of Evolving Systems, Biochemistry & Molecular Biology, and the Pritzker School for Molecular Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL. | 2Department of Molecular and Cellular Physiology and HHMI, Stanford University, Stanford, CA. | 3Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA. | 4Center for Advanced Radiation Sources, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL. | 5Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, and School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA. | 6Modeling and Informatics, Discovery Chemistry, Merck &Co., Inc., South San Francisco, CA

## Abstract

Understanding protein function would be facilitated by direct real-time observation of chemical kinetics in the atomic structure. The selectivity filter (SF) of the K+ channel provides an ideal model, catalyzing the dehydration and transport of K+ ions across the cell membrane through a narrow pore. We used a “pump-probe” method called electric-field stimulated time-resolved X-ray crystallography (EFX) to initiate and observe K+ conduction in the NaK2K channel in both directions on the timescale of the transport process. We observe both known and potentially new features in the high-energy conformations visited along the conduction pathway, including the associated dynamics of protein residues that control selectivity and conduction rate. A single time series of one channel in action shows the orderly appearance of features observed in diverse homologs with diverse methods, arguing for deep conservation of the dynamics underlying the reaction coordinate in this protein family.

## Abstract

Direct visualization of electric field driven ion permeation in a potassium channel exposes a conserved mechanism underlying the reaction coordinate.

## Abstract

Protein function depends on intramolecular mechanics—the local and collective motions of amino acid residues that make up the reaction coordinate 1. To study the mechanism, the most direct approach would be to simply stimulate the functional activity of a protein and watch the resulting pattern of internal motions over time scales consistent with the kinetics of the reaction coordinate. Averaged over many trials, such an experiment would produce atomic resolution snapshots of motions underlying chemical kinetics, exposing a time series of conformations reproducibly visited along the reaction coordinate. These data represent the starting point for building and testing models for the pattern of intramolecular forces controlling the mechanism and constraining the evolution of protein function.

To enable this kind of study, we recently introduced Electric-Field stimulated X-ray crystallography (EFX), a time-resolved pump-probe X-ray diffraction method for protein dynamics 2. EFX involves the application of electric fields in the range of 1 MV/cm to protein crystals to stimulate atomic motions (the pump) followed by brief, intense X-ray pulses (the probe) to read out the protein structure at defined time delays after onset of the electric field (Figure 1A–B). Fields on the order of 1 MV/cm apply subtle forces on all formal and partial charges throughout a protein, biasing conformations by just a few kT. Thus, EFX provides a general route to obtaining atomic structures of the low-lying higher-energy conformational states accessible from the ground state. Carried out as a function of time and averaged over molecules in the diffracting volume, this process enables, in principle, direct visualization of the protein reaction coordinate. For membrane proteins, the electric fields applied are near-physiological, permitting for the first time a study of how changes in transmembrane potential influence protein function.

The potassium (K+) ion channel pore represents an ideal model system to explore the concept of visualizing a reaction coordinate 3. The pore is formed by a symmetric arrangement of four subunits that together form a highly selective, efficient ion conduction pathway at the center (Figure 1C). The basic principles of selective permeation are well-established through a long history of landmark structural and functional studies 3–9 providing an excellent basis for validating dynamical features observed using EFX. The conduction pathway is generally characterized by a wide external vestibule with a binding site for a partially hydrated K+ ion (S0), a narrow selectivity filter forming four binding sites, S1–S4, for fully dehydrated ions, and a central cavity that can hold a hydrated K+ ion (S5) stabilized by through-space electrostatic forces 5,8–10 (Figure 1D). The selectivity filter (SF) of the K+ channel is formed by four loop regions with sequence N’-TVGYG-C’, one from each subunit, with binding sites for ions formed by carbonyl groups that approximate the coordination chemistry of K+ ions by water molecules in bulk solvent 5,9,11. A region immediately below the selectivity filter called the hydrophobic gate appears to partially control conduction rate through interactions with permeating ions 12–14. Conduction amounts to biasing the single-file hopping of K+ ions between binding sites in the selectivity filter by electrochemical gradients to yield a net flux of ions down the gradient 8,9,15,16.

Here, we report an EFX study in which we apply near-physiological electric fields (~0.8 MV/cm, or ~350 mV per channel) directly down the pore axis of the open NaK2K K+ channel in both orientations. NaK2K is a K-selective double mutant of the B. cereus NaK channel, and in recent years has served as a model system for the study of K+ ion permeation 17,18. Using this system, we watch the time-evolution of conformational states and ion hopping in the selectivity filter over a timescale of hundreds of nanoseconds. The data show a rich trajectory of stimulated dynamics in NaK2K, averaged over molecules in the diffracting volume and synchronized by the step-application of the electric field. We observe distinct mechanisms for inward and outward flow of ions, a finding that may originate from field direction-dependent rotational dynamics of the selectivity filter. Many observations made in static structures of diverse K+ channel homologs in various conformations using different methods appear as features in a single time series of one channel during its operation. The data provide a rich basis for refining and testing models for ion permeation and suggest deep conservation of the reaction coordinate in the K+ channel family.

## Results

### EFX experiment design

We carried out EFX experiments at the BioCARS synchrotron facility (Advanced Photon Source, 100ps polychromatic X-ray pulses), custom configured for these specialized time-resolved X-ray diffraction experiments 2,19. Crystals of NaK2K in the open state diffract X rays well (1.7 Å resolution at 292K) and grow as large flat plates in space group I4, with pairs of molecules in the asymmetric unit in head-to-head orientation (molecule A and molecule B in Figure 1C; see also Figure S1F-H). Thus, along the thin dimension of the crystal, channels are positioned upside down relative to the other in each unit cell. By mounting crystals on their flat face to bottom electrodes, we are able to apply electric fields in the range of 1 MV/cm directly down the pore axis, with channels experiencing forces in opposite orientations (Figure 1C). Thus, we can observe electric-field stimulated ion conduction in both directions as a function of time in a single internally controlled experiment.

We carried out an EFX time-series for NaK2K comprising a voltage-OFF initial state, and 100 ns, 200 ns, 500 ns, and 1 μs time delays after onset of a 0.8 MV/cm electric field (Figure 1B). The field rise time is fast (<10 ns, see Methods) compared to the timescale of observation, meaning that observed motions are effectively synchronized by application of the electric field and averaged over the many channel molecules in the diffracting volume. Thus, EFX does not reveal single-molecule atomic motions, but population-averaged snapshots corresponding to the chemical kinetics of the reaction coordinate 20. Since the average rate of ion hopping during conduction through the selectivity filter is expected to be ~100 ns for NaK2K 17,21, the EFX time series covers a range that should reflect relevant conformational states visited during the conduction cycle. We made many improvements that simplify, extend, and generalize the EFX method since its initial report 2, including new electrode designs, remote data collection, and tools for data reduction and analysis. These are briefly summarized in the Methods and Figure S1 and will be formally reported elsewhere.

### The room-temperature ground state

EFX is conducted at ambient temperatures to observe physiological dynamics. Accordingly, we first determined a high-resolution (1.7 Å) reference ground state structure of the NaK2K channel at 292 K (“room temperature”, RT) using a conventional monochromatic synchrotron X-ray source (BL 12–2, SSRL). We refined the structure with initial phases from the published 100 K cryo-structure (PDB 3OUF 17). The RT structure shows excellent overall consistency with the 100 K structure (RMSD of 0.55 Å over all C α atoms), displaying a tetrameric arrangement of subunits, each of which comprises two transmembrane helices (TM1 and TM2), a pore helix, and the loop region between the pore helix and TM2 that forms the selectivity filter (Table S1A). The SF remains highly ordered for both “up” and “down” tetramers (average backbone B-factors of 3.8 and 8.9 Å2 for the selectivity filters of molecules A and B, respectively). Clear densities are observed for the selectivity filter ions. Weak density is observed outside the SF entrance, in line with the SF ions and has been interpreted as an on-axis S0 ion10,17. A partial-occupancy S5 ion is visible at the hydrophobic gate, which based on electron density maps and the position of the F92 side chains, appears to be dehydrated (Figure S3E, F).

To unambiguously determine ion occupancy in the selectivity filter, we collected K+ anomalous scattering data from NaK2K crystals at 100 K and 292 K at low X-ray energy (at 1.46 and 1.49 Å, respectively) enabling us to distinguish ions from water molecules (Figure 2A, Table S1B). The data show that the pore is fully dehydrated and occupied by ions at all sites S1–S4 at both cryo- and room-temperature conditions (Figure 2A–B). This result recapitulates prior findings at cryo-temperatures 18 and shows that the K+ channel pore can support near-full occupancy of ions as one mode of selective transport. At 100K, we also observe four off-axis “S0” K+ binding sites that together add up to unit occupancy. The anomalous scattering data show no clear evidence for an on-axis S0 K+ site at either temperature in NaK2K, suggesting that this site largely represents solvent with weak, if any, occupancy by potassium.

We next studied the relative ground-state affinities of ions for binding sites S1–S4 by determining a series of structures in which we titrated in thallium ions (Tl+) while refining against the Tl+ anomalous signal (Table S1C). Thallium behaves like K+ in terms of selectivity and permeation but produces a greater scattering signal and has a distinct absorption edge that allows us to distinguish this ion from both water and other included ions 22,23. As Tl+ is titrated in, sites with the weakest relative affinity for K+ will be replaced first, and sites with strongest relative affinity will be replaced last. For both channel molecules A and B in the asymmetric unit, the data demonstrate the same heterogeneity and hierarchy of relative binding affinities for Tl+ vs. K+; S1 < S4 < S2 < S3 (Figure 2C). This is also the same order as for refined K+ occupancies at room temperature (Figure 2B), suggesting that the Tl+ titration experiment reflects the hierarchy of intrinsic K+ affinities for sites S1-S4. These findings are consistent with molecular dynamics simulations showing that the S1 and S4 ions are the most labile during the conduction cycle, producing intermediate states with three ions in the selectivity filter and a single vacancy 24. These findings support the “direct knock-on” model for conduction where selective transport of K+ ions involves direct coulombic repulsion between ions, with otherwise high-energy intermediates stabilized by the electrostatic architecture of the selectivity filter 24,25.

The room temperature NaK2K structure also shows that the region in TM2 from Ile86 to Phe92 in the second transmembrane helix adopts two alternate configurations, with occupancies of 63% (conf A) and 37% (conf B) (Figure 2D). In the tetrameric channel, the four Phe92 side chains project into the conduction pathway below the selectivity filter, forming a so-called “hydrophobic gate” that controls conduction rate in NaK2K 13 and in other channel homologs 12,21,26. The alternate conformation of Phe92 was previously at observed at 100 K with similar occupancy 13.

Taken together, analysis of room-temperature ground states of the NaK2K ion channel argues for a dehydrated pore with four ions present at sites S1–S4 with different affinities, and a hydrophobic gate region (I86–F92) with the ability to switch between two alternative conformations. For EFX, these findings provide a basis for interpreting excited state conformations visited upon electric field-induced dynamics.

### The dynamics of ion conduction

To initially study the effects of the applied electric field we used a standard analysis tool in time-resolved crystallography: isomorphous difference maps which show the changes in the electron density around the ground state model upon applying the field (see STAR Methods for a discussion of noise and interpretable detail). Figure 3 shows these maps for the first two timepoints (100 and 200 ns), with green indicating an increase of electron density and red indicating local depletion of electron density; we use letter labels in Figure 3 to connect features to statements below. At 100ns, molecule A, which sees an inward electric field, shows clear evidence for ion permeation in that direction and corresponding movement of the S5 cavity ion. For example, we see depletion of density at (a), new density appearing just below (b), depletion of density at the S2 and above the S1 positions (c), and appearance of new density off-axis near the SF entrance (d). The latter is near the off-axis K+ sites identified in Figure 2A (also see Figure S3G). A pattern of difference density on the sides of the backbone of the SF (e) is consistent with movement of the SF transverse to the pore. At 200 ns, we again see evidence for ion movement in the cavity (f), accompanied by movement of the sidechain of Phe92, the main current-limiting residue (g; this sidechain also shows weak difference density at 100 ns, h). In addition, off-axis features appear in the cavity (j) which we interpret as hydrating waters (see below).

For Molecule B, which sees the electric field in the outward direction, the difference densities are notably different: We see an immediate drop in the occupancy of the S1 ion (k), while the S5 cavity position sees an increase in density at both timepoints (l, m). The selectivity filter exhibits a lateral shift in the opposite direction, most apparent at Gly67 at 100 (n) and 200 ns (p). At 100 ns, Phe92 shows weak positive difference density on the excited state rotamer and negative difference density on the ground state rotamer (q). Positive difference density at the S2 position suggests an upward shift of the S2 ion, possibly partially into the plane of the four carbonyl oxygen atoms (r, s).

Isomorphous difference maps are valuable since they are closest to raw data and minimally subject to bias, but shifts in atomic position, disorder, and occupancy are not always readily distinguished by eye, an issue that is compounded by increased noise near to the fourfold crystallographic symmetry axis. To interpret the observations in more detail, we next refined atomic structures of NaK2K over the complete EFX time series – voltage-OFF, 100 ns, 200 ns, 500 ns, and 1 μs time delays after onset of the electric field (Figure 4A, Tables S2-S3; Figures S3-S4). We carried out refinement of excited states as previously described 2,27–32, with careful iterative refinement against extrapolated structure factors (ESFs) starting from the high-resolution room temperature ground state structure, guided by weighted difference maps and supported by R factor cross-validation statistics (Figures S2, S3, and STAR Methods).

As expected, molecules A and B in the voltage-OFF state are near-identical to their configurations in the reference room temperature structure. However, upon initiation of the electric field, the two molecules show different time- and field orientation-dependent patterns of conformational dynamics, exposing distinct motions associated with ion conduction in both orientations.

Molecule B is oriented such that the electric field drives outward flow of ions (Figure 4B–F), the usual physiological direction for ion flow given the operating membrane potential and the Nernst equilibrium for K+ in most cells. In this direction, the time series shows periodic time-dependent vacancies of the S1 and cavity ions 33. Specifically, the field appears to initially cause a vacancy of the S1 ion at 100ns (Figure 4B–C), leading to a systematic upward hopping of S2–S4 ions and increased density for the S5 cavity ion poised to refill the selectivity filter at 200 ns (Figure 4C–D). Subsequent refilling of the cavity position then triggers additional cycles of field-induced S1 vacancy and single-file ion translocation. The observed timescale of permeation (~200 ns) corresponds to a current of ~1 pA and conductivity of ~3 pS, given estimates of the voltage drop across the channel molecules in the EFX experiment. This value is in the range of the ~10 pS conductance deduced from electrophysiological measurements 17,21 and classical work showing that proteins can function normally in the crystal state with kinetics that are similar to or slightly slower than in solution 34–38. The 500 ns and 1 μs timepoints appear to be averages of the earlier states, suggesting decorrelation of permeation events within the diffracting volume of the crystal over time after the initial synchronizing application of the electric field (Figure 4E–F).

Strikingly, after an initial drop in occupancy due to rapid departure of the S1 ion, the selectivity filter reaches a steady state ion occupancy not much lower than observed at rest (Figure 4, panels B–F). If the selectivity filter remains fully dehydrated as in the voltage-OFF configuration (Figure 2A–B), we deduce that the total occupancy of ions in the selectivity filter varies between three and four ions over the conduction cycle, a finding that is consistent with predictions of the “direct knock-on” model for ion conduction 7,24,39.

Interestingly, the configuration of ions during inward conduction (molecule A, Figure 4G–K) differs substantially from that in the outward process. Inward conduction displays excited states that contain about three ions in the selectivity filter with a tendency towards vacancies of S2 and S4 positions, and multiple states for the cavity ion. The simplest interpretation is that inward conduction involves a transition of the S4 ion into the cavity (Figure 4G) and its stepwise departure (Figure 4G–I), followed by transition of S1–S3 ions downward to partially occupy positions S1, S2, and S4 (Figure 4H–I. 200 ns). The high-affinity S3 site remains fully occupied. The data suggest the S5 cavity ion is dehydrated in the voltage-OFF resting state (Figure S3E, F), but following its shift past the F92 hydrophobic gate, rehydrates with waters appearing nearby at 100 ns (Figure S5I-L) and associating more closely with the departing ion at 200 ns (Figure 4I and S3F). Once again, the ion profiles at 500 ns and 1 μs time delay look like a mixture of earlier states, suggesting re-visitation of these states during multiple cycles of ion transport (Figure 4J–K). These findings are consistent with recent work in the two-pore K+ channel family (K2P) showing mechanistic differences in SF dynamics during inward and outward ion conduction 40. The EFX time series supports a prediction by Schewe et al. that ion occupancies should differ as a function of direction of ion flow.

Targeted sampling of additional time points and mutants may provide a more detailed picture of the reaction coordinate for ion conduction in both directions. Nevertheless, we can already draw one key conclusion: the path of ion conduction is different for opposite directions of ion flow. This result is particularly interesting since available evidence suggests that the single-channel current – voltage (I-V) relationship for NaK2K is symmetric and linear across its reversal potential 17. Thus, the mechanism of conduction differs even though the rate of conduction is the same for inward and outward ion flow. These experimental findings simply remind that mechanism can be degenerate to phenomenology and may contribute to the debates about the generality (or not) of models for ion conduction 7.

### Orientation-dependent rotational dynamics in the selectivity filter

The finding that the path of conduction depends on the direction of ion flow implies some form of structural difference in the non-equilibrium (driven) motions of channel residues as a function of orientation of the applied field. Indeed, the isomorphous difference maps already hint at time-dependent distinct motions of SF amino acids as a function of field orientation (Figure 3). To study this more formally, we analyzed the strain experienced by amino acids in molecules A and B during the initial steps of the EFX time series. Strain is a concept from continuum mechanics that measures the local deformation experienced by a material due to an applied force and is, in general, a more natural and informative measure of “structural change” than simply the displacement of parts of the material 41–43. For example, in comparing two states of a protein molecule, atomic displacements may reflect nearby deformation that underlies the conformational change or simply motions resulting from deformations occurring elsewhere. The analysis of strain separates the two, capturing the local deformations in the environment of any atom in a 3 by 3 tensor whose entries describe various forms of motion (see Methods). For small strains (relative to unity), it is possible to reduce the strain tensor to a scalar value—a pseudo-energy for each atom that gives the magnitude of the structural change between two states of a protein. Strain analysis has been argued to provide important information about basic functional mechanisms in proteins, including allosteric regulation 43.

We computed strain magnitudes at every backbone C α atom for displacements between the voltage-OFF state and the initial 100 ns time delay after onset of the electric field (see Methods). Consistent with the subtlety of the forces applied by the electric field, strain magnitudes are small overall for both molecules A and B (Figure S4) and in the acceptable range for computing pseudo-energies. SF residues display amongst the largest electric field induced strain for both molecules A and B and display an interesting pattern of atomic displacements (Figure 5). The basic result is that the SF undergoes rotational dynamics during ion conduction, where the direction of the rotation switches with the direction of ion flow. For example, in molecule B which shows outward (physiological) ion conduction, the curl of the deformation field (the vector around which the surroundings rotate) points “up”, from the cavity to the extracellular side, meaning that the SF rotates counterclockwise when viewed from the external face (Figure 5A). In molecule A (inward conduction), the curl vector points “down”, from the extracellular surface to the cavity such that the SF rotates clockwise when viewed from the external side (Figure 5B). That is, in both molecules the curl vector points along the electric field. These data suggest that the internal mechanics of the channel transform the electric field into a rotational force field around the central pore, inducing a torque that goes with the direction of ion flow. A plausible model is that this force transmission is mediated by the permeating ions 40; these results now set the stage to determine the causal relationship between SF mechanics and ion permeation.

The rotational deformation of the SF was also observed in strain analyses of ground-state structures of the homologous KcsA K+ channel across different conditions 42, suggesting that this feature is a conserved mechanism in the family of cation channels. The EFX data provide the first direct evidence that these rotational motions are part of the reaction coordinate in these channels. Opposite rotation of the SF for inward and outward conduction is the kind of difference in excited-state dynamics that could explain the observed asymmetry in the mechanism of ion conduction.

These opposite rotations of the SF are also associated with different patterns of strain induced in other regions in the external vestibule of the channel. Residues in the extracellular loop between TM 1 and the pore helix (the so-called “turret” loop, molecule B, Figure 5A) and residues in the loop connecting the external end of the SF to TM 2 (molecule A, Figure 5B) show strains of similar magnitude to that of SF amino acids. Both regions modulate ion conduction through functional allosteric coupling with SF residues in various cation channels. For example, the turret loop controls gating, inactivation, and modulation by lipids in many members of the cation channel family 44–46 and represents part of the binding site for some toxin molecules 47,48 while positions in the loop immediately following the SF mediate block by quaternary cations 49 and regulate the conformational collapse of the SF that underlies one form of channel inactivation 50.

In summary, electric field stimulated ion conduction in both outward and inward directions is associated with a pattern of excited state structural changes that open up new mechanistic hypotheses while also recapitulating known direct and allosteric properties of the K+ channel.

### Deep conservation of mechanism in the cation channel family

The findings that rotational dynamics of the SF are also found in homologs in the cation channel family and that strain develops at conserved allosteric sites motivates examination of the conservation of other features in the EFX time series. Here, we highlight four examples that represent different aspects of channel function during ion conduction:

- The position of the cavity ion varies in a systematic manner in the first 200 ns after onset of the electric field during inward conduction in molecule A, moving from a position proximal to the S4 site to an increasingly distal site. Interestingly, the positions in the voltage-OFF state and at 200 ns time delay recapitulate the cavity ion position observed in the closed and open states, respectively, of the KcsA 9 and MthK channels 51 (Figure 6A, Figure S3E, F).

- We find limited evidence for a low-occupancy conformational flip of the V64–G65 peptide bond in the SF at the 100 ns and 500 ns time points in the EFX time series (Figure 6B; new carbonyl oxygen location +3.1σ in both isomorphous difference maps); this change removes a coordinating carbonyl group from the conduction pathway. Such a flip of the valine carbonyl group has been observed in molecular dynamics simulations of the MthK, KcsA, TREK-1, and TREK-2 ion channels, where it underlies pauses in permeation 52–55. Interestingly, the same conformational flip is also observed in a mutational variant of the KcsA channel (E71A) that shows reduced K+ selectivity and one form of channel inactivation 56 (Figure 6C-D).

- We observe rotamer dynamics of H96, a residue located at the intracellular entrance of the pore, in molecule A at the 100 ns time point (Figure 6E and Figure S5F−G). A similar rotamer flip is observed in a mutational variant (E92Q) at the analogous position in the MthK channel 12; this mutation eliminates a weak K+ coordination site that is thought to enhance conduction by locally concentrating K+ ions at the entry of the permeation pathway.

- Finally, we return to the hydrophobic gate comprising residues I86–F92, the region displaying two alternative configurations in the room-temperature ground state (Figure 1D). In the EFX time series, we find clear evidence for time-evolving shifts in the relative occupancy of the two rotameric states of F92 in apparent concert with movement of the K+ ion at the S5 position, consistent with contraction of the pore radius during the conduction process 13 (Figure 6F and Figure S5). These data support the idea of a dynamical coupling between ion conduction and a collective two-state conformational switch of the I86–F92 hydrophobic gate observed in Figure 2D 12,26,57–60.

These findings lead us to draw a simple conclusion: features observed in various studies of different cation channel homologs using different methods are found in conformational states visited in the EFX experiment, a single time-series of one channel during its operation. These results are even more meaningful given that NaK2K itself is a K+ selective mutational variant of NaK 17, a non-selective member of the cation channel family. These results strongly suggest that the basic dynamical mechanism of ion conduction revealed in the EFX time series is likely to be deeply conserved in members of the cation channel protein family.

## Conclusion

A basic tenet of biochemistry is that the reaction coordinate of proteins is defined by the pattern of orderly dynamical transitions between a few energetically low-lying states near to the ground state. Here, using EFX to excite and visualize these states as they occur in real time, we expose the mechanism of ion conduction in a K+ selective channel in both directions. We find that inward and outward conduction follow different mechanisms, associated with opposite rotations of the selectivity filter. Interestingly, this finding immediately suggests a mechanism by which evolution could tune the rate of inward and outward ion flow independently by adjusting the relative compliance of the SF to the two directions of rotation 61. This process may be the basis for the wide variance in the degree of rectification in different members of the cation channel family. More generally, it will be interesting to use EFX to better understand the connection between selectivity filter mechanics and key properties of channels such as selectivity, rectification, gating, and inactivation.

Many studies have focused on mechanisms of ion conduction in K+ channels with the main debate centered around archetypical models in which permeating ions are either strictly interleaved with water molecules (soft knock-on) or permitted to occupy adjacent positions in selectivity sites (direct knock-on) 7. The data presented here certainly argue that the filter can support adjacent ions. Indeed, the data show that in the resting state of NaK2K, the SF is essentially fully occupied by K+ ions, consistent with the hard knock-on model (Figures 2A-C and 4B). Having said this, the fact that inward and outward permeation in the same channel display different configurations of ions in the excited states argues for a more subtle picture than simply resolving the archetypical models. The data suggest that a distribution of mechanisms may be possible depending on how forces between atoms in the channel shape the energetics of non-equilibrium trajectories of ion permeation in response to an applied electrochemical gradient. These forces are in turn specified by the amino acid sequence, subject to change as conditions of selection potentially vary amongst homologs of the cation channel family. Thus, the generality of models for ion permeation would seem to ultimately depend on the degree to which the mechanical properties of the SF are conserved over the evolution of the cation channel family.

These considerations highlight a role for experimental molecular dynamics that goes beyond simply exposing reaction mechanisms in specific cases. The motivating concept of EFX is that the structures and dynamical transitions within the native state ensemble (the ground and low-lying excited states) will define the evolutionarily programmed reaction coordinate(s) for any protein. In this regard, the finding that features observed in the EFX time series of the NaK2K channel recur in other cation channel homologs speaks directly to the conservation (and therefore functional relevance) of the mechanisms exposed here for ion conduction in the cation channel family. A deeper test of this concept will come with EFX time series of other sequence-diverged channel homologs to directly examine what is invariant and what is idiosyncratic in molecules that diverged from a common ancestor. Such studies may also help to explain how and why statistical models based on amino acid sequences comprising a protein family provide deep information about physical mechanisms within individual proteins, enabling new interpretations, protein engineering, and de novo design 62–68. We propose that the invariances (or “symmetries”) over an ensemble of homologs will represent the core design principles of proteins, with more idiosyncratic features providing for fine tuning of phenotypes for particular cellular contexts or environments.

Recent advances in instrumentation and computational data analysis have significantly simplified and made more robust the experimental process relative to our earlier work 2. The data reported here were collected using a permanent setup for EFX maintained and offered with technical support by the BioCARS facility for macromolecular dynamics (Advanced Photon Source (APS), Argonne National Laboratory). Through BioCARS, the EFX experiment is available via the APS general user program to all members of the scientific community. The data were analyzed, in part, with new software tools specifically designed for reducing and processing time-resolved diffraction data, with more advances under development 69–72. Regardless, practical limitations in densely sampling high-resolution dynamical trajectories over many samples remain and will continue to represent challenges to a purely experimental approach to defining protein reaction coordinates. In this regard, it seems essential to use the kind of datasets presented here to validate and refine atomistic molecular simulation methods to enable a virtuous cycle between simulation and experiment for understanding the physics of protein function73.

### Limitations of the study

The main complexity of all time-resolved pump-probe X-ray diffraction methods for experimental protein dynamics (including EFX) is the difficulty of isolating relatively weak signals from the many sources of random and systematic noise. In general, reaction initiation (the “pump”) only partially populates excited states, requiring the use of special analytic methods such as extrapolated structure factors to visualize excited state structures. This is especially true for methods such as EFX which by design aim to introduce only subtle perturbations (of few kBT) to the ground state. While necessary, these analytic methods come with their own challenges, amplifying measurement noise and making interpretation of traditional crystallographic statistics (e.g. R-factors) and difference electron density maps more complex (see Methods). In addition, in the current electrode configuration, the electric field direction is parallel to the axis of rotation during data collection, causing a few reflections to be inherently unmeasurable, primarily at high resolution. More specific to this work, crystallographic averaging over the four-fold axis in the K+ channel pore may also suggest as symmetric what could be asymmetric intermediates, e.g., in the pattern of rotamer dynamics or ion rehydration in the central cavity. Taken together, these issues compelled us to use a simple molecular model with isotropic B factors to capture the average, essential features of what are likely intricate probabilistic, multi-state, and anisotropic dynamics 7. Finally, crystal preparation and mounting, delivery of electric fields, and reduction/analysis of Laue diffraction data all represent non-standard aspects of the EFX experiment that will continue to evolve as the technique is applied to diverse model systems.

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Protein expression, purification, and crystallization

NaK2K is a double mutant (D66Y and N68D) of the NaK channel of Bacillus cereus and additionally lacks the N-terminal 19 residues17 of the native isoform. The NaK2K gene was cloned with an N-terminal hexahistidine tag into the pQE60 expression vector (Qiagen) and was a gift from Dr. Y. Jiang. NaK2K was expressed, purified, and crystallized as in ref. 17 with any modifications indicated below. The NaK2K construct was transformed into E. coli SG13009 cells (Qiagen; available from the authors upon request), and 1 mL of an overnight culture was used to inoculate 1L of LB media containing 50μg/ml of ampicillin. Cells were grown at 37°C to OD600 = 0.8–1.0, and protein expression was induced by incubation with 0.4 mM IPTG and 5 mM BaCl2 at 25°C overnight. Cells were harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in 13 mL of 100 mM KCl /50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, and stored frozen at −80°C. Frozen cell pellets were first thawed and then lysed by sonication with protease inhibitors (100mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride, 1 μM leupeptin, 1 μM pepstatin). NaK2K protein was extracted from membranes by the addition of 40 mM n-Decyl-β-D-Maltoside (DM) (Anatrace) and incubated for 4 hours at room temperature. The lysate was centrifuged at 21,000 x g for 30 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected and bound to Talon resin (Thermo Scientific) for 1 hour at 4°C. The resin was batch washed with 40ml of 100 mM KCl/50 mM Tris, pH8.0/4mM DM/15mM imidazole until the OD280 of the wash buffer was less than 0.1. NaK2K protein was eluted in 100mM KCl/50mM Tris, pH8.0/4mM DM/300mM imidazole. Thrombin (30 units/2 mg protein, Sigma) was used to remove the hexahistidine tag overnight. Proteolyzed protein was concentrated using a 10 kDa MWCO filtration device (Millipore) followed by size exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200). Fractions containing protein were pooled and concentrated using a 50 kDa MWCO filtration device (Millipore) to OD280 = 8 (~330μM) in 100 mM KCl/4 mM DM/20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0.

NaK2K protein was crystallized by the sitting drop vapor diffusion technique in 100 mM KCl/200 mM potassium citrate tribasic monohydrate/100 mM MES (pH 6.0 or 6.5)/56%−68% (v/v) 2-methyl-2,4-pentanediol (MPD). The crystallization solution forms an aqueous biphasic system with a potassium citrate-rich phase and an MPD-rich phase. The MPD-rich phase (450 μl) was used for the reservoir. Sitting drops were made by mixing the citrate-rich phase mixed with an equal volume of protein (1+1 μl). Crystals grew as flat, square plates (typically, 150 to 400 μm wide) in approximately two weeks at 20oC. This phase separation method produced larger crystals than the reported method due to the presence of potassium citrate.

For experiments using thallium, nitrate ions were substituted for chloride in both protein purification and crystallization by using KNO3 instead of KCl, adjusting pH with HNO3 rather than HCl, and buffering with Tris-HNO3 instead of Tris-HCl. For these experiments, NaK2K protein was mixed with 50 mM MES pH 6.5/100 mM K+-citrate/200 mM TlNO3/56%−68% (v/v) MPD while 50 mM MES pH 6.5/100 mM K+-citrate/200 mM KNO3/56%−68% (v/v) MPD was used for the reservoir. This yielded the “50:50 Tl+:K+” crystals. We then soaked these crystals using two thallium soaking solutions: the first contained 100 mM TlNO3/50 mM MES (pH 6.0 or 6.5)/100 mM Na+-citrate/56%−68% MPD (yielding “50:50 Tl+:Na+” crystals); the second contained 100 mM TlNO3/50 mM MES (pH 6.0 or 6.5)/60%−70% (v/v) MPD (yielding 100% Tl+ crystals). Crystals were transferred to soaking solutions and incubated from 5 minutes to overnight to exchange from K+ to Tl+.

#### Monochromatic data collection and structure refinement

For reference structures, NaK2K crystals were mounted in cryoloops and X-ray diffraction data were collected at several temperatures from 100K to 292K at both the Advanced Photon Source (APS) and at the Stanford Synchrotron Light source (SSRL) (Table S1A-C). Potassium anomalous data were collected at BM-19 beamline SBC-CAT (APS, Argonne National Laboratory). To optimize the anomalous signal, we collected oscillation data in one-degree oscillations over 120 degrees, rotated by 180 degree about the phi axis, and collected over another 120° range. Data were processed using HKL2000 74.

Structure refinement was performed using PHENIX75, with initial phases coming from molecular replacement using the published 100K structure (PDB: 3OUF). We then carried out Cartesian simulated annealing and rounds of xyz refinement, B-factor refinement, water update, and occupancy refinement. Manual adjustments were made using Coot and were supported by Fo-Fc difference maps. Ordinary and anomalous electron density maps were computed in PHENIX. To estimate thallium occupancies, we first assumed that every position was fully occupied by some combination of potassium and thallium ions, while in refinement only Tl+ was modeled. For thallium anomalous data, then, we then estimate true thallium occupancy by the following: O C C T l + r N T l + = O C C T l + t N T l + + ( 1 − O C C T l + t ) N K + , where O C C r refers to refined occupancy and O C C t refers to the true (inferred) occupancy; N T l + and N K + refer to the number of electrons for the indicated ions.

#### EFX sample preparation

EFX experiments were performed at BioCARS (Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National Laboratory) as described2, with several improvements that will be described elsewhere (manuscript in preparation). Briefly, individual NaK2K crystals were mounted by hand on bottom electrodes (Figure S1A-E) inside a humidified (> 90%) chamber to minimize physical stresses due to dehydration. These bottom electrodes were based on a new “solid state” design, in which crystals are in direct contact with a tungsten wire surface to optimize delivery of the electric field and minimize osmotic changes. Bottom electrodes were fabricated by threading tungsten wire (41 μm diameter) into a glass microcapillary (0.018 in O.D., 0.0035 in I.D., 16 mm length; Drummond) and fusing the glass around the tungsten in the flame of a Bunsen burner. The protruding wires at the melted ends of the capillaries were trimmed before the electrode tips were hand-polished, using a series of fine grit sandpapers until the surface was flat and glass and metal were flush (Figure S1B).

Crystals were placed on the polished end of the bottom electrode and glued down using partially precured Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer (see below) by draping this glue around the crystal using a thin fishing line, taking care to not encase the crystal in the elastomer. The electrode assembly with mounted crystal was then enclosed in a polyester sleeve (MiTeGen, Inc.) containing a mixture (20μL) of 50:50 crystallization solution and water to clamp humidity while the glue fully cured. We apply High Vacuum Grease (Dow Corning) around the polyester sleeve and goniobase to minimize humidity fluctuations. Curing times were at least 8 hours. We also refined a new top electrode design which enables us to pass the electrode through the crystallization/water solution in the polyester sleeve of the bottom electrode, picking up a drop of this solution for crystal contact to establish the electrical circuit for field delivery (Figure S1E). This process minimizes osmotic pressure differences that may disrupt crystal lattice order. To establish the final configuration, the bottom electrode was fitted to the goniometer, and a top electrode positioned using a three-axis micromanipulator with camera-assisted guidance (Figure S1D-E).

#### Sylgard preparation

Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Curing agent (Dow Chemical) was mixed with Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Base (Dow Chemical) in a 1:10 ratio. After mixing, the uncured glue was degassed for 20 minutes, aliquoted into PCR tubes and placed in a gradient PCR machine to near-cure. The following protocol was used: 5 minutes at 4°C, 48 minutes with a gradient from 45.5 to 47.5°C, and a final hold at 4°C. Partially cured Sylgard 184 was stored at −80°C until use for crystal gluing.

#### Data Collection

The data collection protocol was as described in ref. 2 with the following modifications. At each crystal orientation, we first collected an X-ray diffraction image without electric field (‘voltage-OFF’) and then we collected electric-field stimulated data at desired delays from the start of the electric field pulse (Figure 1B), with one second delays to permit crystal relaxation. Data were collected for all time points at a particular crystal orientation, then repeated for each rotation. The data reported here were collected from 0° to 184° in 4° steps, then offset 2° and again collected in 4° steps. X-ray pulses had 100ps duration and energy bandwidth of 5%. High-voltage pulses were generated using a custom designed dual-polarity high-voltage pulse generator from FID GmbH (Burbach, Germany).

The data display a completeness similar to previous high-quality time-resolved diffraction data in the range > 2.2 Å, but a few factors led to less completeness in the highest resolution shell (2.2 – 2.0 Å, see Table S4): (1) the beam center was slightly off-center, (2) the c-axis of the crystal lattice was aligned (by design) with the axis of rotation during data collection, rendering a portion of the reciprocal-space unit cell unobservable, primarily at high resolution, (3) Precognition/Epinorm tends to reject observations in the 2.0 and 2.2 Å range deemed “noisy” but are nevertheless of high quality (average I/sigI > 10, Table S3), (4) the need to observe both ‘ON’ and ‘OFF’ structures factors in computing extrapolated structure factors (row 3 in Table S4), and (5) existence of a statistical filter in PHENIX not quite suitable for extrapolated structure factors (row 4 in Table S4).

An analysis of inclusion thresholds applied during scaling and merging (as well as two different scaling modes that differ in their treatment of harmonic reflections) is provided for the 100 and 200 ns timepoints (Table S5). This analysis shows that completeness can be substantially increased by lowering the inclusion threshold, albeit with a gentle increase in R factors with completeness (keeping existing R-free flags and adding new ones for new reflections proportionally). Thus, the deposited models are not overfit. Calculation of F o − F c difference maps with these more complete data provide further support for the appearance of waters surrounding the departing S5 ion in molecule A at 100 ns (Figure S5, panels I-L; 5.0 σ peak in the F o − F c map). In addition, evidence improves (to 3.9 σ) for increased occupancy of an excited-state rotamer for I86 in molecule B, consistent with observations in Figure 2D.

#### EFX data reduction and refinement

Laue diffraction data were processed using Precognition (Renz Research) and Epinorm76, with local scaling, and calculated extrapolated structure factors, F e x t , and weighted difference maps were calculated using custom scripts (MATLAB, Mathworks Inc.) as previously described 2. Briefly, weights for each map coefficient were calculated as 1 / ( 1 + σ 2 ( Δ F ) 〈 σ 2 ( Δ F ) 〉 + ( Δ F ) 2 / 〈 ( Δ F ) 2 〉 ) , where 〈 … 〉 denotes averages over Miller indices and errors σ ( Δ F ) in structure factor amplitudes were calculated by adding error estimates for F o b s O N and F o b s O F F in quadrature for observed structure factor amplitudes in the presence ( F o b s O N ) and absence ( F o b s O F F ) . To model the timepoints in the presence of the electric field, extrapolated structure factor amplitudes were calculated as F E S F = N ( F o b s O N − F o b s O F F ) + F o b s O F F with N = 8 for all timepoints. Initial phases were derived from the deposited EFX ‘OFF’ structure. Map coefficients were calculated in CCP4, and extrapolated structure factors and weighted difference maps were calculated using reciprocalspaceship 72 and Phenix 75. Composite omit maps were calculated using default settings in PHENIX.

Structure refinement was performed using PHENIX 75, starting from the high-resolution monochromatic room temperature (292K) dataset. The voltage-OFF structure in the EFX time series was refined starting from the 292K monochromatic model by molecular replacement, followed by cycles of rigid-body refinement, Cartesian simulated annealing, XYZ refinement, B-factor refinement, occupancy refinement, and manual adjustment. Refinement against these extrapolated structure factor amplitudes started from the OFF model, followed by limited automated refinement such as XYZ refinement, B-factor refinement, and occupancies refinement in PHENIX and manual adjustments in Coot based on F o − F c difference maps. The merit of rounds of refinement was assessed based on R factors (as shown in Figure S3A-D). Ion occupancies were constrained to a maximum of 0.25 if the ion was located along the fourfold symmetry axis. At the end of the refinement process, we performed five cycles of targeted refinement in PHENIX in which subsequently occupancies of the K+ ions were refined (with B factors of each ion fixed to the average B factor of its ‘cage’ of nearest backbone atoms of the selectivity filter) and a round in which the B factors of the selectivity filter and contained K+ ions were refined while keeping occupancies fixed. In this approach, ion B factors stabilized to within about 2 Å2 and occupancies to better than 1 %.

It is worth including a note about the interpretation of R-factors from excited state refinement. In general, the residuals used to calculate R factors consist of two components: measurement error and model error: F o − F c = ( F o − F true ) − ( F c − F true ) . For conventional refinement, R factors are dominated by model errors ( F c − F true ) and therefore are interpreted as representing model quality. However, the use of extrapolated structure factors (ESFs) has the effect of amplifying measurement errors, making the magnitude of associated R factors (1) larger and (2) an unreliable comparative measure of model quality. However, the measurement error component remains constant during refinement, such that changes in R work and R free can guide refinement, as for conventional datasets. We note that several different approaches for computing ESFs have been described 27, including the use of weighted extrapolated factors ( F h E S F = w h N ( F o b s , h O N − F o b s , h O F F ) + F o b s , h O F F ) 2 and extrapolation relative to OFF-state amplitudes ( F E S F = N ( F o b s O N − F o b s O F F ) + F calc O F F ) 77,78. The use of these approaches can make calculated R factors substantially lower (Table S5, bottom row), but we note that these are purely cosmetic manipulations and do not circumvent the issue of amplified measurement noise. For example, the use of weighted ESFs with N = 12 such that 〈 w N 〉 ≈ 8 , gives R w o r k and R f r e e of 17.9 and 17.5%, respectively for the deposited 100ns model with no further refinement.

#### Isomorphous difference maps from time-resolved Laue experiments

Isomorphous difference maps from Laue diffraction data raises a number of unique challenges to accurately correct for systematic errors in estimating structure factors. To validate the process used here, we compared the EFX dataset with that from a single-crystal Laue dataset for photoexcitation in Photoactive Yellow Protein (PYP; described in ref. 69; unmerged as well as scaled and merged data are included in the Zenodo deposition; see Data and code availability), a reference model system for which accurate excited state models are available 79,80. Specifically, we used a dataset comprising 20 dark diffraction images and 20 matching diffraction images collected 2 ms after photoexcitation and processed the data both in Precognition with local scaling and in Careless 69 with default parameter settings, except for use of the robust error model described in ref. 69 to reduce the effect of outliers. Both PYP and EFX datasets display diffraction extending past the edge of the detector. Truncated to 2.0 Å, both datasets are of similar multiplicity (3.49 for the EFX data and 3.65 for PYP), similar completeness of observed reflections (85.7% for the EFX data and 85.3% for PYP), and similar CC1/2 (0.931 for EFX data, 0.899 for PYP; Figure S6A-B).

To validate difference map calculations, we first calculated a model-based ( F c − F c ) map using ground-state and excited-state models of PYP extracted from PDB 1TS0, ref. 79 using structure factors computed with phenix.fmodel. The complex structure factors subtracted using reciprocalspaceship 72 and differences converted back to amplitudes and phases. The ( F c − F c ) map (compare Figures S6C-D) serves a reference for what we should expect from a good experimental ( F o − F o ) difference map. Indeed, the results show that the weighted experimental difference map approach used here is consistent with the ( F c − F c ) map (compare Figures S6D-E, real-space correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.42). We observe a weaker correlation for the unweighted map (real-space CC of 0.23). We conclude that the weighted difference map approach used here provides a good representation of relevant features in the experimental data.

Map-map correlations (CC) were calculated using tools from GEMMI (https://gemmi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html) within a 10 Å-radius of the terminal hydroxyl group of the PYP chromophore. These calculations are described in detail in an accompanying Jupyter notebook (see Zenodo deposition). Calculations of completeness for these datasets are likewise described in accompanying Jupyter notebooks (see Zenodo deposition).
